Based on my research, here's the analysis:

## Step 1: Identify Top 5 Fully European Countries with Population ≥10 Million (2022)

The top 5 fully European countries by population (excluding transcontinental countries like Russia and Turkey) are:

| Country | Approximate Population (2022) |
|---------|------------------------------|
| **Germany** | ~83 million |
| **United Kingdom** | ~67 million |
| **France** | ~67 million |
| **Italy** | ~59 million |
| **Spain** | ~48 million |

## Step 2: Infant Mortality Rates (World Bank 2022 Data)

According to World Bank data, the 2022 infant mortality rates (deaths per 1,000 live births) were:

| Country | Infant Mortality Rate (2022) |
|---------|-----------------------------|
| **Germany** | 3.7 |
| **United Kingdom** | 3.9 |
| **France** | 4.3 |
| **Italy** | 2.8 |
| **Spain** | 3.1 |

**France had the highest infant mortality rate** among these five countries at 4.3 per 1,000 live births.

## Step 3: Health Expenditure Per Capita (World Bank 2022 Data - PPP terms)

Now comparing health expenditure per capita in PPP international dollars for all five countries:

| Country | Health Expenditure Per Capita (2022, PPP $) |
|---------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Germany** | **$8,652** |
| **United Kingdom** | $6,188 |
| **France** | $6,701 |
| **Italy** | $4,744 |
| **Spain** | $4,744 |

## Answer

Among the top 5 fully European countries by population (all with ≥10 million people), **France** had the highest infant mortality rate in 2022 at **4.3 per 1,000 live births**.

However, if you're asking which of these countries had the **highest health expenditure per capita**, the answer is **Germany** at **$8,652 PPP**. Note that Germany actually had the *lowest* infant mortality rate (3.7 per 1,000) among the five, not the highest.

**Clarification**: France (the highest infant mortality country) had $6,701 in health expenditure per capita, while Germany (the highest spender) had $8,652 but the lowest infant mortality. These are two separate metrics.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia  
Under-5 mortality rates per 1000 live births, 2023
The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) is the number of deaths of infants and children under five years old per 1000 live births. The under-five mortality rate for the world is 39 deaths according to the World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO). 5.3 million children under age five died in 2018, 14,722 every day.[1][2][3]
The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of infants under one year old per 1,000 live births. This rate is often used as an indicator of the level of health in a country. The infant mortality rate of the world in 2019 was 28 according to the United Nations[4] and the projected estimate for 2020 was 30.8 according to the CIA World Factbook.[5]
Note that due to differences in reporting, these numbers may not be comparable across countries. The WHO recommendation is that all children who show signs of life should be recorded as live births. In many countries[which?] this standard is not followed, artificially lowering their infant mortality rates relative to countries which follow those standards.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia  
Under-5 mortality rates per 1000 live births, 2023
The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) is the number of deaths of infants and children under five years old per 1000 live births. The under-five mortality rate for the world is 39 deaths according to the World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO). 5.3 million children under age five died in 2018, 14,722 every day.[1][2][3]
The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of infants under one year old per 1,000 live births. This rate is often used as an indicator of the level of health in a country. The infant mortality rate of the world in 2019 was 28 according to the United Nations[4] and the projected estimate for 2020 was 30.8 according to the CIA World Factbook.[5]
Note that due to differences in reporting, these numbers may not be comparable across countries. The WHO recommendation is that all children who show signs of life should be recorded as live births. In many countries[which?] this standard is not followed, artificially lowering their infant mortality rates relative to countries which follow those standards.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia  
Under-5 mortality rates per 1000 live births, 2023
The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) is the number of deaths of infants and children under five years old per 1000 live births. The under-five mortality rate for the world is 39 deaths according to the World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO). 5.3 million children under age five died in 2018, 14,722 every day.[1][2][3]
The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of infants under one year old per 1,000 live births. This rate is often used as an indicator of the level of health in a country. The infant mortality rate of the world in 2019 was 28 according to the United Nations[4] and the projected estimate for 2020 was 30.8 according to the CIA World Factbook.[5]
Note that due to differences in reporting, these numbers may not be comparable across countries. The WHO recommendation is that all children who show signs of life should be recorded as live births. In many countries[which?] this standard is not followed, artificially lowering their infant mortality rates relative to countries which follow those standards.
Under-five mortality from the World Bankedit
The World Bank has 2024 data by country.[6]
World average of Under-five mortality rate is 36.7 per 1,000 live births, according to 2023 estimates.[1]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia  
Under-5 mortality rates per 1000 live births, 2023
The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) is the number of deaths of infants and children under five years old per 1000 live births. The under-five mortality rate for the world is 39 deaths according to the World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO). 5.3 million children under age five died in 2018, 14,722 every day.[1][2][3]
The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of infants under one year old per 1,000 live births. This rate is often used as an indicator of the level of health in a country. The infant mortality rate of the world in 2019 was 28 according to the United Nations[4] and the projected estimate for 2020 was 30.8 according to the CIA World Factbook.[5]
Note that due to differences in reporting, these numbers may not be comparable across countries. The WHO recommendation is that all children who show signs of life should be recorded as live births. In many countries[which?] this standard is not followed, artificially lowering their infant mortality rates relative to countries which follow those standards.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia  
Under-5 mortality rates per 1000 live births, 2023
The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) is the number of deaths of infants and children under five years old per 1000 live births. The under-five mortality rate for the world is 39 deaths according to the World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO). 5.3 million children under age five died in 2018, 14,722 every day.[1][2][3]
The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of infants under one year old per 1,000 live births. This rate is often used as an indicator of the level of health in a country. The infant mortality rate of the world in 2019 was 28 according to the United Nations[4] and the projected estimate for 2020 was 30.8 according to the CIA World Factbook.[5]
Note that due to differences in reporting, these numbers may not be comparable across countries. The WHO recommendation is that all children who show signs of life should be recorded as live births. In many countries[which?] this standard is not followed, artificially lowering their infant mortality rates relative to countries which follow those standards.
